[[Category:new pages]]
'''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank}}. In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|平清盛}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In qq60 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

[[Category:Completion tier 2]] '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank}}. In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|平清盛}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In qq60 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

[[Category:Completion tier 2]] '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank}}. In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|公卿|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|平清盛}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

[[Category:Completion tier 2]] '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank}}. In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.

Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.

Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. [[Category:Pages to be written]] '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank}}. In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

[[Category:Court Ranks of Japan]][[Category:completion tier 4]] '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-ranks/court-ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

[[Category:Court Ranks of Japan]][[Category:completion tier 4]][[Category: tier 4]] '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-ranks/court-ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-ranks/court-ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.

'''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=draft}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai|12=draft}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=draft}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=draft}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-ranks/court-ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=draft}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=draft}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon|12=draft}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=draft}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言|12=draft}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=draft}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=draft}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori|12=draft}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱|12=draft}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議|12=draft}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=draft}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=draft}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣|12=draft}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長|12=draft}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|12=draft}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=draft}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階|12=draft}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=draft}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.
== References ==

revision.text:
'''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=draft}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai|12=draft}} in Japan. It ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=draft}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=draft}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-ranks/court-ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=draft}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=draft}}). These ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon|12=draft}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=draft}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言|12=draft}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=draft}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=draft}}.
Over time, as rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This rank, originally intended for higher-ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori|12=draft}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱|12=draft}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議|12=draft}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=draft}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=draft}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣|12=draft}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長|12=draft}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|12=draft}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=draft}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|ranks of nobility|ja|位階|12=draft}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=draft}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

{{出典の明記|date=2015年8月}} '''正三位'''（しょうさんみhttps://kotobank.jp/word/正三位）とは、[[位階]]及び[[神階]]のひとつ。[[従二位]]の下、[[従三位]]の上に位する。日本では「おおきみつのくらい」｢おおいみつのくらい｣とも読む。 == 概要 == [[律令制]]下においては、従三位以上を「貴」と称し、また「星の位」ともいわれ、[[公卿|上級貴族]]の位階であった。従三位が[[中納言]]や[[近衛大将]]、大宰帥などと[[官位相当]]であるのに対し、正三位は[[大納言]]相当とされた。[[勲等]]との対比では[[勲一等]]に値する。 時代が下るにつれ、官位相当によらない叙位任官も増え、官位相当の大納言は[[従二位]]、[[近衛大将|大将]]・[[近衛府|中将]]も二位及び三位で運用されたため、中納言でこの位階に叙せられる例も少なくなかった。これにより、本来、上位の位階である筈の正三位も比較的中堅公卿の位階として定着するようになったのをはじめ、本来は堂上となる筈のなかった武家も、中央政界の争乱への関与と貢献を重ねるうちに身分を上昇させ、正三位またはその前後への位階に昇る例が見られるようになった。 武家政治の創始者ともいうべき[[平清盛]]の官途はその先駆的な例であり、[[永暦]]元年([[1160年]])、前年の平治の乱で宿敵 源氏の棟梁 源義朝を打倒した清盛は武士として初の正三位となり、[[参議]]兼[[兵衛府|右兵衛督]]となりさらに官途を重ねて最終的に[[従一位]][[太政大臣]]となった。清盛の嫡男 [[平重盛|重盛]]が正三位参議を経て後に正二位[[内大臣]]となり、重盛の死後、清盛の後継に擁立された三男 [[平宗盛|宗盛]]もまた正三位参議を経て、最終的に従一位[[内大臣]]となった。清盛四男の[[平知盛|知盛]]は正三位[[中納言|権中納言]]を経て従二位に、五男の[[平重衡|重衡]]は従三位[[近衛府|左近衛中将]]より正三位となった。 [[鎌倉時代]]以降となると、正三位は[[征夷大将軍]]またはその世子が昇叙の段階で上る位階となり、[[鎌倉幕府]]二代将軍の[[源頼家]]が[[将軍宣下]]前に[[衛門府|左衛門督]]に[[任官]]した際この正三位に叙せられ、その弟 三代将軍 [[源実朝]]は[[兵衛府|右兵衛佐]][[従五位|従五位下]]で叙爵と同時に征夷大将軍を宣下された後、昇叙を重ね正三位行右近衛中将に昇った後に、最終的に[[右大臣]][[正二位]]まで上り詰めた。その次代である[[摂家将軍]][[藤原頼経]]も[[正五位|正五位下]]を初叙とした他は実朝とほぼ同じ[[位階]]で昇進を重ね、正三位権中納言を経て、最終的に[[正二位]][[大納言|権大納言]]となっている。 その後、[[皇族]]が将軍となる[[宮将軍]]がしばらく続いたことから、人臣の位階たる[[武家]]への正三位叙位はしばらく途絶えたものの、[[後醍醐天皇]]による[[北条高時]]追討により[[鎌倉幕府]]が滅亡すると、建武元年([[1335年]])、[[足利尊氏]]が正三位参議兼[[兵衛府|左兵衛督]]となる例が見られた。しかし、[[足利将軍家]]の位階が正二位内大臣で定着するようになると、将軍及びその世子の官途も従三位からいきなり[[従二位]]へと昇る例が増え、正三位への叙位は四代将軍 [[足利義持|義持]]とその弟 [[足利義嗣]]、九代将軍 [[足利義尚|義尚]]が官途のさなかに正三位への叙位がなされた例に留まった。 戦国時代後期以降では織田信長が安土城を完成させた、天正4年([[1576年]])、正三位に昇ったのをはじめ、織田信長嫡孫 [[織田秀信]]は正三位権中納言となり、信長四男で[[豊臣秀吉]]の養子となった[[羽柴秀勝]]も秀信と同じ官位を授けられた他、秀吉の弟 [[豊臣秀長]]、[[徳川家康]]が正三位を経て従二位へと昇叙する例が見られたが、高位ということもあり、武家の叙位にあっては、正三位叙位の発令は決して多いというものではなかった。 [[江戸時代]]以降では、正三位はほぼ徳川将軍家または一門の当主のみが昇る位階となったが、それでも決して叙位例は多いとはいえず、240年の江戸時代の歴史の中で、将軍となった者に対する正三位への叙位は三代将軍 徳川家光が初叙で正三位となった他、五代将軍綱吉が[[承応]]2年（[[1653年]]）、元服した年に[[従四位|従四位下]]から正三位に昇叙し後に参議に任官、後に六代将軍となる徳川家宣も甲州藩主時代の[[延宝]] 8年([[1680年]])に正三位参議となった例に留まった（将軍世子は、そもそも初叙が従二位となり、他家から将軍になった者であっても、従三位から正三位を経ずに正二位に昇る。）。 また、徳川一門でも正三位への叙位は特殊であったとさえいえ、家康次男で越前福井藩初代藩主の結城秀康は生前正三位であった他、御三家でも家康九男 徳川義直にはじまる尾張藩歴代十七代の藩主のうち、二代 徳川光友が正三位権中納言から権大納言、従二位へと昇り、三代 [[徳川綱誠|綱誠]]がこれにならう形で正三位に叙せられただけに留まり、紀州藩でも歴代藩主十四代のうち、正三位に叙せられた例は二代藩主 [[徳川光貞|光貞]]が正三位権中納言を経て後に従二位権大納言となった他は、十四代藩主 [[徳川茂承|茂承]]だけであった。 近代以降、正三位の位階は[[華族]]の爵位における[[伯爵]]の初叙位階とされた他、[[陸軍大将]]、[[海軍大将]]などが叙せられる位階となった。[[西郷隆盛]]は生前に正三位に叙せられるも[[西南戦争]]において官位を褫奪され「賊軍の将」とされたが、[[大日本帝国憲法]]発布による大赦により赦され、改めて正三位を贈られることで名誉回復がなされた。今日では、位階が物故者を対象とする栄典となったのに伴い、[[国務大臣]]経験者の他、政府の重要[[官職]]にあった者、学術分野において多大な功労ある人物が死後に叙せられるのが通例となっている。芸術・芸能分野で正三位に叙せられる例は、極めて少ない。 '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine Rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine Rank)=Shinkai (divine Rank)|lt=shinkai|12=draft|12=draft}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=draft|12=draft}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=draft|12=draft}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft|12=draft}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=draft|12=draft}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=draft|12=draft}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft|12=draft}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon|12=draft|12=draft}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=draft|12=draft}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言|12=draft|12=draft}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=draft|12=draft}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=draft|12=draft}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft|12=draft}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|12=draft|12=draft}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori|12=draft|12=draft}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝|12=draft|12=draft}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱|12=draft|12=draft}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議|12=draft|12=draft}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=draft|12=draft}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=draft|12=draft}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣|12=draft|12=draft}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長|12=draft|12=draft}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|12=draft|12=draft}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=draft|12=draft}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Ranks of nobility|ja|位階|12=draft|12=draft}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=draft|12=draft}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft|12=draft}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Ranks of nobility|ja|位階|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

{{出典の明記|date=2015年8月}} '''正三位'''（しょうさんみhttps://kotobank.jp/word/正三位）とは、[[位階]]及び[[神階]]のひとつ。[[従二位]]の下、[[従三位]]の上に位する。日本では「おおきみつのくらい」｢おおいみつのくらい｣とも読む。 == 概要 == [[律令制]]下においては、従三位以上を「貴」と称し、また「星の位」ともいわれ、[[公卿|上級貴族]]の位階であった。従三位が[[中納言]]や[[近衛大将]]、大宰帥などと[[官位相当]]であるのに対し、正三位は[[大納言]]相当とされた。[[勲等]]との対比では[[勲一等]]に値する。 時代が下るにつれ、官位相当によらない叙位任官も増え、官位相当の大納言は[[従二位]]、[[近衛大将|大将]]・[[近衛府|中将]]も二位及び三位で運用されたため、中納言でこの位階に叙せられる例も少なくなかった。これにより、本来、上位の位階である筈の正三位も比較的中堅公卿の位階として定着するようになったのをはじめ、本来は堂上となる筈のなかった武家も、中央政界の争乱への関与と貢献を重ねるうちに身分を上昇させ、正三位またはその前後への位階に昇る例が見られるようになった。 武家政治の創始者ともいうべき[[平清盛]]の官途はその先駆的な例であり、[[永暦]]元年([[1160年]])、前年の平治の乱で宿敵 源氏の棟梁 源義朝を打倒した清盛は武士として初の正三位となり、[[参議]]兼[[兵衛府|右兵衛督]]となりさらに官途を重ねて最終的に[[従一位]][[太政大臣]]となった。清盛の嫡男 [[平重盛|重盛]]が正三位参議を経て後に正二位[[内大臣]]となり、重盛の死後、清盛の後継に擁立された三男 [[平宗盛|宗盛]]もまた正三位参議を経て、最終的に従一位[[内大臣]]となった。清盛四男の[[平知盛|知盛]]は正三位[[中納言|権中納言]]を経て従二位に、五男の[[平重衡|重衡]]は従三位[[近衛府|左近衛中将]]より正三位となった。 [[鎌倉時代]]以降となると、正三位は[[征夷大将軍]]またはその世子が昇叙の段階で上る位階となり、[[鎌倉幕府]]二代将軍の[[源頼家]]が[[将軍宣下]]前に[[衛門府|左衛門督]]に[[任官]]した際この正三位に叙せられ、その弟 三代将軍 [[源実朝]]は[[兵衛府|右兵衛佐]][[従五位|従五位下]]で叙爵と同時に征夷大将軍を宣下された後、昇叙を重ね正三位行右近衛中将に昇った後に、最終的に[[右大臣]][[正二位]]まで上り詰めた。その次代である[[摂家将軍]][[藤原頼経]]も[[正五位|正五位下]]を初叙とした他は実朝とほぼ同じ[[位階]]で昇進を重ね、正三位権中納言を経て、最終的に[[正二位]][[大納言|権大納言]]となっている。 その後、[[皇族]]が将軍となる[[宮将軍]]がしばらく続いたことから、人臣の位階たる[[武家]]への正三位叙位はしばらく途絶えたものの、[[後醍醐天皇]]による[[北条高時]]追討により[[鎌倉幕府]]が滅亡すると、建武元年([[1335年]])、[[足利尊氏]]が正三位参議兼[[兵衛府|左兵衛督]]となる例が見られた。しかし、[[足利将軍家]]の位階が正二位内大臣で定着するようになると、将軍及びその世子の官途も従三位からいきなり[[従二位]]へと昇る例が増え、正三位への叙位は四代将軍 [[足利義持|義持]]とその弟 [[足利義嗣]]、九代将軍 [[足利義尚|義尚]]が官途のさなかに正三位への叙位がなされた例に留まった。 戦国時代後期以降では織田信長が安土城を完成させた、天正4年([[1576年]])、正三位に昇ったのをはじめ、織田信長嫡孫 [[織田秀信]]は正三位権中納言となり、信長四男で[[豊臣秀吉]]の養子となった[[羽柴秀勝]]も秀信と同じ官位を授けられた他、秀吉の弟 [[豊臣秀長]]、[[徳川家康]]が正三位を経て従二位へと昇叙する例が見られたが、高位ということもあり、武家の叙位にあっては、正三位叙位の発令は決して多いというものではなかった。 [[江戸時代]]以降では、正三位はほぼ徳川将軍家または一門の当主のみが昇る位階となったが、それでも決して叙位例は多いとはいえず、240年の江戸時代の歴史の中で、将軍となった者に対する正三位への叙位は三代将軍 徳川家光が初叙で正三位となった他、五代将軍綱吉が[[承応]]2年（[[1653年]]）、元服した年に[[従四位|従四位下]]から正三位に昇叙し後に参議に任官、後に六代将軍となる徳川家宣も甲州藩主時代の[[延宝]] 8年([[1680年]])に正三位参議となった例に留まった（将軍世子は、そもそも初叙が従二位となり、他家から将軍になった者であっても、従三位から正三位を経ずに正二位に昇る。）。 また、徳川一門でも正三位への叙位は特殊であったとさえいえ、家康次男で越前福井藩初代藩主の結城秀康は生前正三位であった他、御三家でも家康九男 徳川義直にはじまる尾張藩歴代十七代の藩主のうち、二代 徳川光友が正三位権中納言から権大納言、従二位へと昇り、三代 [[徳川綱誠|綱誠]]がこれにならう形で正三位に叙せられただけに留まり、紀州藩でも歴代藩主十四代のうち、正三位に叙せられた例は二代藩主 [[徳川光貞|光貞]]が正三位権中納言を経て後に従二位権大納言となった他は、十四代藩主 [[徳川茂承|茂承]]だけであった。 近代以降、正三位の位階は[[華族]]の爵位における[[伯爵]]の初叙位階とされた他、[[陸軍大将]]、[[海軍大将]]などが叙せられる位階となった。[[西郷隆盛]]は生前に正三位に叙せられるも[[西南戦争]]において官位を褫奪され「賊軍の将」とされたが、[[大日本帝国憲法]]発布による大赦により赦され、改めて正三位を贈られることで名誉回復がなされた。今日では、位階が物故者を対象とする栄典となったのに伴い、[[国務大臣]]経験者の他、政府の重要[[官職]]にあった者、学術分野において多大な功労ある人物が死後に叙せられるのが通例となっている。芸術・芸能分野で正三位に叙せられる例は、極めて少ない。 '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Ranks of nobility|ja|位階|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Ranks of nobility|ja|位階|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

{{出典の明記|date=2015年8月}} '''正三位'''（しょうさんみhttps://kotobank.jp/word/正三位）とは、[[位階]]及び[[神階]]のひとつ。[[従二位]]の下、[[従三位]]の上に位する。日本では「おおきみつのくらい」｢おおいみつのくらい｣とも読む。 == 概要 == [[律令制]]下においては、従三位以上を「貴」と称し、また「星の位」ともいわれ、[[公卿|上級貴族]]の位階であった。従三位が[[中納言]]や[[近衛大将]]、大宰帥などと[[官位相当]]であるのに対し、正三位は[[大納言]]相当とされた。[[勲等]]との対比では[[勲一等]]に値する。 時代が下るにつれ、官位相当によらない叙位任官も増え、官位相当の大納言は[[従二位]]、[[近衛大将|大将]]・[[近衛府|中将]]も二位及び三位で運用されたため、中納言でこの位階に叙せられる例も少なくなかった。これにより、本来、上位の位階である筈の正三位も比較的中堅公卿の位階として定着するようになったのをはじめ、本来は堂上となる筈のなかった武家も、中央政界の争乱への関与と貢献を重ねるうちに身分を上昇させ、正三位またはその前後への位階に昇る例が見られるようになった。 武家政治の創始者ともいうべき[[平清盛]]の官途はその先駆的な例であり、[[永暦]]元年([[1160年]])、前年の平治の乱で宿敵 源氏の棟梁 源義朝を打倒した清盛は武士として初の正三位となり、[[参議]]兼[[兵衛府|右兵衛督]]となりさらに官途を重ねて最終的に[[従一位]][[太政大臣]]となった。清盛の嫡男 [[平重盛|重盛]]が正三位参議を経て後に正二位[[内大臣]]となり、重盛の死後、清盛の後継に擁立された三男 [[平宗盛|宗盛]]もまた正三位参議を経て、最終的に従一位[[内大臣]]となった。清盛四男の[[平知盛|知盛]]は正三位[[中納言|権中納言]]を経て従二位に、五男の[[平重衡|重衡]]は従三位[[近衛府|左近衛中将]]より正三位となった。 [[鎌倉時代]]以降となると、正三位は[[征夷大将軍]]またはその世子が昇叙の段階で上る位階となり、[[鎌倉幕府]]二代将軍の[[源頼家]]が[[将軍宣下]]前に[[衛門府|左衛門督]]に[[任官]]した際この正三位に叙せられ、その弟 三代将軍 [[源実朝]]は[[兵衛府|右兵衛佐]][[従五位|従五位下]]で叙爵と同時に征夷大将軍を宣下された後、昇叙を重ね正三位行右近衛中将に昇った後に、最終的に[[右大臣]][[正二位]]まで上り詰めた。その次代である[[摂家将軍]][[藤原頼経]]も[[正五位|正五位下]]を初叙とした他は実朝とほぼ同じ[[位階]]で昇進を重ね、正三位権中納言を経て、最終的に[[正二位]][[大納言|権大納言]]となっている。 その後、[[皇族]]が将軍となる[[宮将軍]]がしばらく続いたことから、人臣の位階たる[[武家]]への正三位叙位はしばらく途絶えたものの、[[後醍醐天皇]]による[[北条高時]]追討により[[鎌倉幕府]]が滅亡すると、建武元年([[1335年]])、[[足利尊氏]]が正三位参議兼[[兵衛府|左兵衛督]]となる例が見られた。しかし、[[足利将軍家]]の位階が正二位内大臣で定着するようになると、将軍及びその世子の官途も従三位からいきなり[[従二位]]へと昇る例が増え、正三位への叙位は四代将軍 [[足利義持|義持]]とその弟 [[足利義嗣]]、九代将軍 [[足利義尚|義尚]]が官途のさなかに正三位への叙位がなされた例に留まった。 戦国時代後期以降では織田信長が安土城を完成させた、天正4年([[1576年]])、正三位に昇ったのをはじめ、織田信長嫡孫 [[織田秀信]]は正三位権中納言となり、信長四男で[[豊臣秀吉]]の養子となった[[羽柴秀勝]]も秀信と同じ官位を授けられた他、秀吉の弟 [[豊臣秀長]]、[[徳川家康]]が正三位を経て従二位へと昇叙する例が見られたが、高位ということもあり、武家の叙位にあっては、正三位叙位の発令は決して多いというものではなかった。 [[江戸時代]]以降では、正三位はほぼ徳川将軍家または一門の当主のみが昇る位階となったが、それでも決して叙位例は多いとはいえず、240年の江戸時代の歴史の中で、将軍となった者に対する正三位への叙位は三代将軍 徳川家光が初叙で正三位となった他、五代将軍綱吉が[[承応]]2年（[[1653年]]）、元服した年に[[従四位|従四位下]]から正三位に昇叙し後に参議に任官、後に六代将軍となる徳川家宣も甲州藩主時代の[[延宝]] 8年([[1680年]])に正三位参議となった例に留まった（将軍世子は、そもそも初叙が従二位となり、他家から将軍になった者であっても、従三位から正三位を経ずに正二位に昇る。）。 また、徳川一門でも正三位への叙位は特殊であったとさえいえ、家康次男で越前福井藩初代藩主の結城秀康は生前正三位であった他、御三家でも家康九男 徳川義直にはじまる尾張藩歴代十七代の藩主のうち、二代 徳川光友が正三位権中納言から権大納言、従二位へと昇り、三代 [[徳川綱誠|綱誠]]がこれにならう形で正三位に叙せられただけに留まり、紀州藩でも歴代藩主十四代のうち、正三位に叙せられた例は二代藩主 [[徳川光貞|光貞]]が正三位権中納言を経て後に従二位権大納言となった他は、十四代藩主 [[徳川茂承|茂承]]だけであった。 近代以降、正三位の位階は[[華族]]の爵位における[[伯爵]]の初叙位階とされた他、[[陸軍大将]]、[[海軍大将]]などが叙せられる位階となった。[[西郷隆盛]]は生前に正三位に叙せられるも[[西南戦争]]において官位を褫奪され「賊軍の将」とされたが、[[大日本帝国憲法]]発布による大赦により赦され、改めて正三位を贈られることで名誉回復がなされた。今日では、位階が物故者を対象とする栄典となったのに伴い、[[国務大臣]]経験者の他、政府の重要[[官職]]にあった者、学術分野において多大な功労ある人物が死後に叙せられるのが通例となっている。芸術・芸能分野で正三位に叙せられる例は、極めて少ない。 '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Ranks of nobility|ja|位階|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

'''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|ja|神階|Shinkai (divine rank)=Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shinkai|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Middle Counsellor|ja|中納言|1=Chūnagon|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Senior Counsellor|ja|大納言|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
{{ill|Taira no Kiyomori|ja|Taira no Kiyomori|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|ja|源義朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the {{ill|Heiji Rebellion|ja|平治の乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Councillor|ja|参議|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Grand Chancellor|ja|太政大臣|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|ja|藤原道長|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Ranks of nobility|ja|位階|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.
