<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11123261]] Wikidata name: Senior Third Rank [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility in Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=court rank in Japan|WD=Q99196082}} and [[:en:Shinkai (divine rank)|shinkai]] in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|qq=}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the [[:en:Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Ranks|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Commander of the Imperial Guards|1=Konoe Daisho|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638972}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to [[:en:Dainagon|Senior Counsellor]]. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Orders of merit in Japan|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Class of Merit|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 勲等|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
[[Taira no Kiyomori]]{{citation needed |Taira no Kiyomori|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Kiyomori|qq=}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]] during the [[:en:Heiji rebellion|Heiji Rebellion]], Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed [[:en:Sangi (Japan)|Sangi]] and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Right Guard Commander|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 衛門府|1=Emonfu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11626338}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Juni'i|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and ultimately held the position of [[:en:Daijō-daijin|Grand Chancellor]].
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, [[:en:Fujiwara no Michinaga|Fujiwara no Michinaga]], a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoritomo|Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Court Ranks in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the [[:en:Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11123261]] Wikidata name: Senior Third Rank [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility in Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=court rank in Japan|WD=Q99196082}} and [[:en:Shinkai (divine rank)|shinkai]] in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|qq=}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the [[:en:Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Ranks|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Commander of the Imperial Guards|1=Konoe Daisho|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638972}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to [[:en:Dainagon|Senior Counsellor]]. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Orders of merit in Japan|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Class of Merit|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 勲等|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
[[Taira no Kiyomori]]{{citation needed |Taira no Kiyomori|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Kiyomori|qq=}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]] during the [[:en:Heiji rebellion|Heiji Rebellion]], Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed [[:en:Sangi (Japan)|Sangi]] and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Right Guard Commander|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 衛門府|1=Emonfu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11626338}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Juni'i|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and ultimately held the position of [[:en:Daijō-daijin|Grand Chancellor]].
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, [[:en:Fujiwara no Michinaga|Fujiwara no Michinaga]], a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoritomo|Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Court Ranks in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the [[:en:Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q11123261]] Wikidata name: Senior Third Rank [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:11, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} '''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility in Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=court rank in Japan|WD=Q99196082}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|en|Shinkai (divine rank)|WD=Q11591025|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|qq=}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|WD=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Ranks|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Commander of the Imperial Guards|1=Konoe Daisho|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638972}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Senior Counsellor}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Orders of merit in Japan|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Class of Merit|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 勲等|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
[[Taira no Kiyomori]]{{citation needed |Taira no Kiyomori|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Kiyomori|qq=}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|en|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|WD=Q532301|lt=Minamoto no Yoshitomo}} during the {{ill|Heiji rebellion|en|Heiji rebellion|WD=Q944859|lt=Heiji Rebellion}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Sangi (Japan)|en|Sangi (Japan)|WD=Q1133663|lt=Sangi}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Right Guard Commander|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 衛門府|1=Emonfu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11626338}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Juni'i|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Daijō-daijin|en|Daijō-daijin|WD=Q1157586|lt=Grand Chancellor}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|WD=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Court Ranks in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|WD=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:正三位]][[ko:정3위]][[zh:正三位]]
'''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility in Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=court rank in Japan|WD=Q99196082}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|en|Shinkai (divine rank)|WD=Q11591025|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|qq=}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|WD=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Ranks|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Commander of the Imperial Guards|1=Konoe Daisho|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638972}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Senior Counsellor}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Orders of merit in Japan|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Class of Merit|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 勲等|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
[[Taira no Kiyomori]]{{citation needed |Taira no Kiyomori|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Kiyomori|qq=}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|en|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|WD=Q532301|lt=Minamoto no Yoshitomo}} during the {{ill|Heiji rebellion|en|Heiji rebellion|WD=Q944859|lt=Heiji Rebellion}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Sangi (Japan)|en|Sangi (Japan)|WD=Q1133663|lt=Sangi}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Right Guard Commander|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 衛門府|1=Emonfu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11626338}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Juni'i|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Daijō-daijin|en|Daijō-daijin|WD=Q1157586|lt=Grand Chancellor}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|WD=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Court Ranks in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|WD=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

'''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility in Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Court Ranks in Japan|WD=Q99196082}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|en|Shinkai (divine rank)|WD=Q11591025|lt=shinkai|1=Shinkai (divine rank)}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|qq=}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|WD=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system|1=Ritsuryō}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Ranks|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Commander of the Imperial Guards|1=Konoe Daisho|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638972}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Senior Counsellor|1=Dainagon}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Orders of merit in Japan|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Class of Merit|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 勲等|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
[[Taira no Kiyomori]]{{citation needed |Taira no Kiyomori|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Kiyomori|qq=}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|en|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|WD=Q532301|lt=Minamoto no Yoshitomo|1=Minamoto no Yoshitomo}} during the {{ill|Heiji rebellion|en|Heiji rebellion|WD=Q944859|lt=Heiji Rebellion|1=Heiji rebellion}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Sangi (Japan)|en|Sangi (Japan)|WD=Q1133663|lt=Sangi|1=Sangi (Japan)}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Right Guard Commander|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 衛門府|1=Emonfu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11626338}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Juni'i|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Daijō-daijin|en|Daijō-daijin|WD=Q1157586|lt=Grand Chancellor|1=Daijō-daijin}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|WD=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga|1=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|1=Minamoto no Yoritomo}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Court Ranks in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|WD=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system|1=Ritsuryō}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

'''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Ranks of nobility in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility in Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Court Ranks in Japan|WD=Q99196082}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|en|Shinkai (divine rank)|WD=Q11591025|lt=shinkai|1=Shinkai (divine rank)}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|1=Junior Third Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|qq=}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|WD=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system|1=Ritsuryō}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Ranks|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Commander of the Imperial Guards|ja|近衛大将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Commander of the Imperial Guards|1=Konoe Daisho|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638972}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Senior Counsellor|1=Dainagon}}. In comparison with {{ill|Orders of merit in Japan|ja|勲等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Orders of merit in Japan|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|First Class of Merit|ja|勲一等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Class of Merit|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 勲等|1=Japanese honors system|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17990718}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|nobles|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|senior aristocracy|ja|Kugyō|1=Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|1=Kugyō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3138036}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
[[Taira no Kiyomori]]{{citation needed |Taira no Kiyomori|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Kiyomori|qq=}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|en|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|WD=Q532301|lt=Minamoto no Yoshitomo|1=Minamoto no Yoshitomo}} during the {{ill|Heiji rebellion|en|Heiji rebellion|WD=Q944859|lt=Heiji Rebellion|1=Heiji rebellion}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Sangi (Japan)|en|Sangi (Japan)|WD=Q1133663|lt=Sangi|1=Sangi (Japan)}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Right Guard Commander|ja|右衛門督|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Right Guard Commander|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 衛門府|1=Emonfu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11626338}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Juni'i|ja|従二位|1=Junior Second Rank|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Juni'i|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Daijō-daijin|en|Daijō-daijin|WD=Q1157586|lt=Grand Chancellor|1=Daijō-daijin}}.
== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|WD=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga|1=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|1=Minamoto no Yoritomo}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.

Although the system of {{ill|Court Ranks in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

== Historical Figures ==
Several notable individuals were appointed to Shōsanmi during the Heian and Kamakura periods. Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|qid=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga|1=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|qid=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|1=Minamoto no Yoritomo}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance. Posthumous promotions were not uncommon, especially for individuals whose contributions were considered significant to the state or society.
== Modern Usage ==
Although the system of {{ill|Court Ranks in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} was abolished during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治改革|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Restoration|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the historical significance of titles such as Shōsanmi continues to be studied and referenced in academic and cultural contexts. The Rank is often mentioned in historical records, literary works, and discussions of Japan’s feudal systems. Contemporary historians analyze the Rank’s evolution to understand the social mobility and political structures of the time.
== Cultural Impact ==
The Rank of Shōsanmi, like other titles in the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|qid=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system|1=Ritsuryō}}, played a role in the cultural identity of Japan’s aristocracy. It symbolized prestige and recognition, often serving as an aspiration for families aiming to elevate their social status. The influence of the Rank extended beyond the court to domains such as literature, art, and ceremonial traditions, reflecting its integration into the broader fabric of Japanese society.

'''Shōsanmi''' (正三位) is one of the {{ill|Court Ranks in Japan|ja|位階|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ranks of nobility in Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q99196082}} and {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|en|Shinkai (divine rank)|qid=Q11591025|lt=shinkai}} in Japan. It Ranks below {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and above {{ill|Junior Third Rank|ja|従三位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Third Rank|qq=}}. <ref>https://www.wakapoetry.net/background/society/court-offices-titles-and-Ranks/court-Ranks/</ref>In Japan, it is also read as "Ōkimitsunokurai" or "Ōimitsunokurai" <ref name="kotobank">https://kotobank.jp/word/正三位</ref>.
== Overview ==
Under the {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|qid=Q742460|lt=Ritsuryō system}}, individuals of Jusanmi or higher were referred to as "Noble" ({{ill|Ki|ja|貴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ki|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) and also called "Star Ranks" ({{ill|Star Ranks|ja|星の位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Ranks|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}). These Ranks belonged to the {{ill|Kugyō|ja|Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3138036}}. While Jusanmi was equivalent to {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|qid=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon}} or {{ill|Konoe Daisho|ja|近衛大将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Commander of the Imperial Guards|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11638972}}, Shōsanmi corresponded to {{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|qid=Q1354706|lt=Senior Counsellor}}. In comparison with {{ill|Japanese honors system|ja|勲等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Orders of merit in Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17990718}}, it was equivalent to {{ill|Japanese honors system|ja|勲一等|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Class of Merit|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 勲等|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17990718}}.
Over time, as Rank promotions and appointments deviated from strict adherence to official Rank equivalencies, instances of middle-level {{ill|Kugyō|ja|Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3138036}} being promoted to Shōsanmi became more common. This Rank, originally intended for higher-Ranking aristocrats, came to be seen as a mid-level Rank for {{ill|Kugyō|ja|Kugyō|2=ja|3=公卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/senior aristocracy|13=User:Immanuelle/Kugyō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3138036}}. Furthermore, samurai families that were traditionally not part of the court nobility gradually rose to positions within or near the Shōsanmi Rank through their involvement in and contributions to central political affairs.
[[Taira no Kiyomori]]{{citation needed |Taira no Kiyomori|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Taira no Kiyomori|qq=}}, a pivotal figure in the rise of samurai governance, is a leading example of this shift. In 1160 (Eiryaku 1), after defeating his rival {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|en|Minamoto no Yoshitomo|qid=Q532301|lt=Minamoto no Yoshitomo}} during the {{ill|Heiji rebellion|en|Heiji rebellion|qid=Q944859|lt=Heiji Rebellion}}, Kiyomori became the first samurai to attain the Rank of Shōsanmi. He was appointed {{ill|Sangi (Japan)|en|Sangi (Japan)|qid=Q1133663|lt=Sangi}} and concurrently served as {{ill|Emonfu|ja|右衛門督|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Right Guard Commander|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 衛門府|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11626338}}. He later advanced to {{ill|Junior Second Rank|ja|従二位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Juni'i|13=User:Immanuelle/Junior Second Rank|qq=}} and ultimately held the position of {{ill|Daijō-daijin|en|Daijō-daijin|qid=Q1157586|lt=Grand Chancellor}}.
== Historical Figures ==

Among these figures were poets, military leaders, and court officials whose influence shaped Japan's history. For instance, {{ill|Fujiwara no Michinaga|en|Fujiwara no Michinaga|qid=Q433133|lt=Fujiwara no Michinaga}}, a prominent aristocrat during the Heian period, held the Rank of Shōsanmi before ascending to higher Ranks. Michinaga’s political dominance and literary contributions solidified his legacy as one of the era's most influential figures.
Additionally, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|en|Minamoto no Yoritomo|qid=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo}}, the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|ja|鎌倉導带|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura shogunate|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, was posthumously awarded Shōsanmi, reflecting the recognition of his achievements in establishing samurai governance.
